以下に、次のAIチャットにそのまま貼り付けられる引き継ぎ文書を作成します。

---

# プロジェクト引き継ぎ文書

## 基本情報

私は千葉大学の学部4年生（B4）で、大川研究室に所属しています。卒業研究として**「空間音響を伴う裸眼立体映像インタラクションシステム」**を開発しています。これまでTouchDesignerで実装を進めてきましたが、**Leap Motionによる接触インタラクションの実装効率・処理速度を考慮し、Unityに移行することを決定しました。**

---

## 研究の目的・概要

### システム全体の目的

- **裸眼立体視（Fish Tank VR）**：ペッパーズゴースト方式（天井型LCD＋45度ハーフミラー）で空中に浮かんで見える裸眼立体映像を表示する
- **視点追従（オフアクシス投影）**：Webカメラ＋MediaPipeで顔（鼻）の位置を検出し、ユーザーの視点に合わせてリアルタイムにカメラ投影を変化させる（Fish Tank VR）
- **空間音響（HRTF/バイノーラル）**：3D空間内の音源（対象物）とリスナー（ユーザーの頭）の位置関係から、イヤホンでバイノーラル再生される立体音響を生成する
- **Leap Motionハンドインタラクション**：ユーザーの手・指の3D座標を取得し、空中に浮かんで見える対象物に「触れる」操作を実現する
- **接触時のマルチモーダルフィードバック**：触れた瞬間に「音が鳴る（聴覚フィードバック）」「モデルが変形する（視覚フィードバック）」ことで、距離感・接触感をより直感的に伝える

### 研究の新規性の軸

1. **視点追従（Fish Tank VR）× 空間音響の統合的検証**
2. **低コストWebカメラ式装置への統合システム**

### 対象モチーフ

**カエル**を選定。理由：
- 定期的に鳴くことで「そこにある」という聴覚的立体表現が自然に成立する
- 触ると鳴く＋変形するという聴覚・視覚フィードバックの組み合わせが、接触時の距離感把握に効果的
- 実世界のオブジェとして置いてあっても違和感がない
- 接触反応（凹む・縮む）の設計が生物的で直感的

---

## TouchDesignerで実装済みの内容

### 1. 視点追従（MediaPipe → CameraExt Pan/Dolly制御）

**概要**：WebカメラからMediaPipeで顔のランドマーク（鼻・耳）を検出し、フレーム間の差分をカメラのPan/Dollyに反映するシステムを構築済み。

**実装の核心**：
- `null1`（`nose:x`, `nose:y`, `left_ear:x`, `right_ear:x`, `left_ear:y`, `right_ear:y`）
- `null3`（`nose:z`, `left_ear:z`, `right_ear:z`）
- `execute1`（Execute DAT）で毎フレーム差分計算 → `cameraViewport.ext.CameraExt.StartTransform/Transform/EndTransform()`でカメラ操作

**重要な知見**：
- TouchDesignerの`mediapipe['nose:x']`は`td.Channel`型を返すため、`float()`変換が必要
- `parent.Camera`は`cameraViewport`内部でのみ有効、外部からは`op('/project1/cameraViewport')`で参照
- MediaPipeの座標は`left_ear`/`right_ear`のラベルが反転している（左右を入れ替えて使う必要がある）
- x/y座標は符号を反転させる必要がある（カメラ座標系との違い）
- Z方向は高周波ノイズが大きいため、指数移動平均（EMA）によるスムージングが必須
- フレーム間の異常値除外（`max_delta`による上限クランプ）も必須（暴走防止）

**調整パラメータ**（`cameraViewport`のカスタムパラメータページ「Mediapipe」に追加済み）：
- `Pansensitivity`（X/Y感度、デフォルト3.0）
- `Dollysensitivity`（Z感度、デフォルト2.0）
- `Panthreshold`（X/Yデッドゾーン、デフォルト0.0005）
- `Dollythreshold`（Zデッドゾーン、デフォルト0.002）
- `Zsmoothing`（Zスムージング係数、デフォルト0.1）
- `Maxdelta`（異常値除外しきい値、デフォルト0.05）
- `Invertx`（左右反転トグル）

### 2. 空間音響リスナー位置（MediaPipe耳座標 → listenerHead COMP）

**概要**：カメラのPan/Dolly（相対・累積制御）とは独立して、MediaPipeの左右耳座標から頭の絶対位置・向きを直接計算し、`listenerHead`（Null COMP）に毎フレーム反映するシステムを構築済み。

**実装の核心**：
- `execute_listener`（Execute DAT）で毎フレーム実行
- 左右耳の中点 → `listenerHead`の`tx, ty, tz`（頭の位置）
- 左右耳を結ぶベクトルのatan2 → `listenerHead`の`ry`（頭の向き）
- 座標変換：MediaPipeの正規化座標（-0.5〜0.5程度） → ワールド座標（スケール×10程度）
- Z方向も同様にEMAスムージング適用
- `earMarker_L`/`earMarker_R`（Geometry COMP）で耳の位置を3Dビュー上に可視化

**調整パラメータ**（`listenerHead`のカスタムパラメータページ「Audio」に追加済み）：
- `Scalexy`（XY倍率、デフォルト10.0）
- `Scalez`（Z倍率、デフォルト40.0）
- `Basedistance`（基準距離、デフォルト2.5）
- `Zoffset`（Z基準点、デフォルト0.2855）
- `Invertx`（左右反転トグル）

### 3. 空間音響パイプライン（Audio Render CHOP + Steam Audio）

**概要**：`Audio Oscillator CHOP`（仮の音源）→ `Audio Render CHOP`（Steam Audio、Simple Positional、Binaural出力）→ `Audio Device Out CHOP` という構成で、3D空間の音源とリスナーの位置関係から自動的にバイノーラル音声を生成するパイプラインを構築済み。

**Audio Render CHOPの設定**：
- `Mode`: Simple Positional
- `Output Format`: Binaural
- `Listener Object COMP`: `/project1/listenerHead`
- `Object COMP`（音源）: `/project1/GEOS/SPHERE`
- `Enable Attenuation`: On（距離による音量減衰）

**重要な知見**：
- TouchDesignerには「Audio Spatial CHOP」という名前のCHOPは存在しない
- `Audio Binaural CHOP`は「すでにマルチチャンネルミックスされた音声をバイノーラルに変換するもの」で、3D音源配置には使わない
- 3D音源配置は`Audio Render CHOP`（Steam Audio内蔵）が担う
- `Audio Oscillator`は`chan1`の1チャンネルしか出力しないため、`Audio Binaural CHOP`（2ch以上必要）とは相性が悪い。`Audio Render CHOP`なら直接接続可能

### 4. 音量メーター可視化（左右バランス確認用）

- `Audio Render`の出力 → `Math CHOP`（Positive/絶対値化）→ `Filter CHOP`（平滑化）
- 左用・右用の`Rectangle TOP`を2つ作成し、`Composite TOP`で並べて表示
- 目的：左右の空間音響パンニングが正しく機能しているかを視覚的に確認するため

---

## Unityで実装すべき内容（今後の作業）

### フェーズ1（最優先）：視点追従（Fish Tank VR）の再実装

TouchDesignerで動作確認済みのMediaPipe→オフアクシス投影を、Unityで再実装する。

**必要な要素**：
- Webカメラ映像の取得（Unity側でのカメラデバイス制御）
- MediaPipeによる顔ランドマーク検出（`nose:x/y/z`, `left_ear:x/y/z`, `right_ear:x/y/z`）
  - UnityでMediaPipeを使う方法：[MediaPipe Unity Plugin](https://github.com/homuler/MediaPipeUnityPlugin)が主流
- オフアクシス投影（非対称視錐台）の実装
  - Unityの`Camera.projectionMatrix`を毎フレーム書き換える方式
  - 頭の位置（耳座標の中点）から`left/right/top/bottom/near/far`を計算してMatrixを構成
- 重要な実装詳細（TouchDesignerでの知見より）：
  - 耳座標のラベルは反転している（left/rightを入れ替えて使う）
  - x/y座標の符号反転が必要
  - Z方向は高周波ノイズが大きいためEMAスムージング必須
  - フレーム間の差分に上限クランプ（異常値除外）が必要

### フェーズ2：カエルの3Dモデル準備

**方針**：デフォルメされたロウポリ調のカエルを用意し、後のLeap Motion接触変形に対応しやすい構成にする。

**構成パーツ案**（変形単位で分けておくと後が楽）：
- 胴体（Body）
- 頭（Head）
- 目×2（Eye_L, Eye_R）
- 後脚×2（LegBack_L, LegBack_R、大きめ）
- 前脚×2（LegFront_L, LegFront_R、小さめ）

**選択肢**：
- Unityのプリミティブ（Sphere, Capsule等）の組み合わせ
- Blender等でモデリングしてFBXインポート
- フリー素材のカエル3Dモデル（Sketchfab等）

### フェーズ3：空間音響の再実装（HRTF/バイノーラル）

**方針**：UnityにはSteam Audio Unity Plugin（無料）があり、TouchDesignerで実現したのと同等以上のバイノーラル空間音響をより簡単に実装できる。

**必要な要素**：
- [Steam Audio Unity Plugin](https://valvesoftware.github.io/steam-audio/doc/unity/)の導入
- `Steam Audio Source`コンポーネントをカエルのGameObjectに追加（音源位置）
- `Steam Audio Listener`コンポーネントをカメラ（リスナー）に追加
- リスナー位置をMediaPipeの耳座標（`listenerHead`相当）から毎フレーム更新するスクリプト
- 距離による音量減衰の設定（Steam Audioの`Attenuation`機能）

### フェーズ4：カエルの鳴き声（定期的な発音）

- カエルの鳴き声音源の調達（フリー素材推奨：Freesound.org等で「frog call」等で検索）
- Unityの`AudioSource`を`AudioClip`でトリガーする仕組み（`PlayOneShot`等）
- 不規則な間隔でのトリガー（`Coroutine`＋`WaitForSeconds(Random.Range(min, max))`等）

### フェーズ5：Leap Motionの接続と接触検出

- Ultraleap（旧Leap Motion）の最新SDKは**Gemini（v5）**、Unityプラグインは[Ultraleap Unity Plugin](https://github.com/ultraleap/UnityPlugin)
- 手・指の3D座標をUnityのワールド座標として取得
- カエルの各パーツ（Collider）との距離計算で「触れた」を判定
- 接触判定の閾値はTouchDesignerの`Dollythreshold`/`Panthreshold`相当のパラメータとして外部からチューニングできるようにする

### フェーズ6：接触時のマルチモーダルフィードバック

**音**：接触判定が発生した瞬間に`AudioSource.PlayOneShot(frogCallClip)`でカエルの鳴き声を発音  
**変形**：接触したパーツのTransformのScaleを一時的に縮小する（`LeanTween`や`DOTween`等のアニメーションライブラリを使うと数行で実装できる）

---

## 参考論文・キーワード（研究背景）

- **Fish Tank VR**：Ware et al. (1993)、head-coupled perspective
- **HRTF/空間音響**：Zahorik (2022, Frontiers in Neuroscience)
- **Pseudo-haptics（接触時の視覚フィードバック）**：PLOS ONE (2016)
- **視覚的捕捉（visual capture / ventriloquist effect）**
- **キーワード**：visual capture, ventriloquist effect, pseudo-haptics, HRTF, motion parallax, integral imaging, fish tank VR, presence, SUS, NASA-TLX, Presence Questionnaire

---

## 現在の優先課題

1. **UnityでMediaPipe Unity Pluginを導入し、`nose:x/y/z`と`left_ear:x/y/z`/`right_ear:x/y/z`が正しく取得できることを確認する**
2. **Unityのカメラの`projectionMatrix`をオフアクシス（非対称視錐台）に毎フレーム書き換えるスクリプトを実装し、Fish Tank VRの視点追従が動作することを確認する**
3. その後、Steam Audio Unity Pluginを導入し、空間音響のパイプラインを組む

---

以上です。このまま新しいAIチャットに貼り付ければ、プロジェクトの全体像・これまでの成果・今後のタスクが即座に伝わります。Unity移行後の実装で行き詰まった点があれば、具体的なコードや設定値の提示を求めてください。

# Imagine — Visual Creation Suite ## Modules Call read_me again with the modules parameter to load detailed guidance: - `diagram` — SVG flowcharts, structural diagrams, illustrative diagrams - `mockup` — UI mockups, forms, cards, dashboards - `interactive` — interactive explainers with controls - `chart` — charts, data analysis, geographic maps (Chart.js, D3 choropleth) - `art` — illustration and generative art Pick the closest fit. The module includes all relevant design guidance. **Complexity budget — hard limits:** - Box subtitles: ≤5 words. Detail goes in click-through (`sendPrompt`) or the prose below — not the box. - Colors: ≤2 ramps per diagram. If colors encode meaning (states, tiers), add a 1-line legend. Otherwise use one neutral ramp. - Horizontal tier: ≤4 boxes at full width (~140px each). 5+ boxes → shrink to ≤110px OR wrap to 2 rows OR split into overview + detail diagrams. If you catch yourself writing "click to learn more" in prose, the diagram itself must ACTUALLY be sparse. Don't promise brevity then front-load everything. **Accessibility:** For HTML widgets, begin with a visually-hidden `

` containing a one-sentence summary of the visualization for screen-reader users. (SVG widgets use `role="img"` with `` and `<desc>` instead — see SVG setup.) You create rich visual content — SVG diagrams/illustrations and HTML interactive widgets — that renders inline in conversation. The best output feels like a natural extension of the chat. ## Core Design System These rules apply to ALL use cases. ### Philosophy - **Seamless**: Users shouldn't notice where claude.ai ends and your widget begins. - **Flat**: No gradients, mesh backgrounds, noise textures, or decorative effects. Clean flat surfaces. - **Compact**: Show the essential inline. Explain the rest in text. - **Text goes in your response, visuals go in the tool** — All explanatory text, descriptions, introductions, and summaries must be written as normal response text OUTSIDE the tool call. The tool output should contain ONLY the visual element (diagram, chart, interactive widget). Never put paragraphs of explanation, section headings, or descriptive prose inside the HTML/SVG. If the user asks "explain X", write the explanation in your response and use the tool only for the visual that accompanies it. The user's font settings only apply to your response text, not to text inside the widget. ### Streaming Output streams token-by-token. Structure code so useful content appears early. - **HTML**: `<style>` (short) → content HTML → `<script>` last. - **SVG**: `<defs>` (markers) → visual elements immediately. - Prefer inline `style="..."` over `<style>` blocks — inputs/controls must look correct mid-stream. - Keep `<style>` under ~15 lines. Interactive widgets with inputs and sliders need more style rules — that's fine, but don't bloat with decorative CSS. - Gradients, shadows, and blur flash during streaming DOM diffs. Use solid flat fills instead. ### Rules - No `<!-- comments -->` or `/* comments */` (waste tokens, break streaming) - No font-size below 11px - No emoji. Icons = Tabler **outline** webfont (5800+, already loaded): `<i class="ti ti-home"></i>`. Outline only — never use `-filled` suffixes (`ti-heart-filled` etc. are not loaded and will render blank). Inherits color + font-size from parent. Decorative icons get `aria-hidden="true"`; icon-only buttons get `aria-label`. Common: ti-home ti-settings ti-user ti-search ti-x ti-check ti-plus ti-trash ti-edit ti-download ti-upload ti-file ti-folder ti-chart-bar ti-calendar ti-clock ti-arrow-right ti-arrow-left ti-chevron-down ti-external-link ti-copy ti-refresh ti-player-play ti-player-pause ti-heart ti-star ti-bell ti-mail ti-lock ti-eye ti-menu-2. Don't hand-draw icon SVG paths. - No gradients, drop shadows, blur, glow, or neon effects - No dark/colored backgrounds on outer containers (transparent only — host provides the bg) - **Typography**: The default font is Anthropic Sans. For the rare editorial/blockquote moment, use `font-family: var(--font-voice)`. - **Headings**: h1 = 22px, h2 = 18px, h3 = 16px — all `font-weight: 500`. Heading color is pre-set to `var(--text-primary)` — don't override it. Body text = 16px, weight 400, `line-height: 1.7`. **Two weights only: 400 regular, 500 bold.** Never use 600 or 700 — they look heavy against the host UI. - **Sentence case** always. Never Title Case, never ALL CAPS. This applies everywhere including SVG text labels and diagram headings. - **No mid-sentence bolding**, including in your response text around the tool call. Entity names, class names, function names go in `code style` not **bold**. Bold is for headings and labels only. - The widget container is `display: block; width: 100%`. Your HTML fills it naturally — no wrapper div needed. Just start with your content directly. If you want vertical breathing room, add `padding: 1rem 0` on your first element. - Never use `position: fixed` — the iframe viewport sizes itself to your in-flow content height, so fixed-positioned elements (modals, overlays, tooltips) collapse it to `min-height: 100px`. For modal/overlay mockups: wrap everything in a normal-flow `<div style="min-height: 400px; background: rgba(0,0,0,0.45); display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;">` and put the modal inside — it's a faux viewport that actually contributes layout height. - No DOCTYPE, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` — just content fragments. - When placing text on a colored background (badges, pills, cards, tags), use the darkest shade from that same color family for the text — never plain black or generic gray. - **Corners**: use `border-radius: var(--radius)` for controls, `12px` for cards. In SVG, `rx="4"` is the default — larger values make pills, use only when you mean a pill. - **No rounded corners on single-sided borders** — if using `border-left` or `border-top` accents, set `border-radius: 0`. Rounded corners only work with full borders on all sides. - **No titles or prose inside the tool output** — see Philosophy above. - **Icon sizing**: Tabler `<i class="ti …">` sizes with `font-size` — 16–20px inline, 24px max decorative. For one-off inline SVG icons, set `width`/`height` explicitly (same limits). - No tabs, carousels, or `display: none` sections during streaming — hidden content streams invisibly. Show all content stacked vertically. (Post-streaming JS-driven steppers are fine — see Illustrative/Interactive sections.) - No nested scrolling — auto-fit height. - Scripts execute after streaming — load libraries via `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` (UMD globals), then use the global in a plain `<script>` that follows. The library `<script src>` tag must come BEFORE any inline script that uses its global — never call a library from code that appears above its `<script src>` tag. - **CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external resources may ONLY load from `cdnjs.cloudflare.com`, `esm.sh`, `cdn.jsdelivr.net`, `unpkg.com`, `fonts.googleapis.com`, `fonts.gstatic.com`. All other origins are blocked by the sandbox — the request silently fails. ### CSS Variables **Surfaces**: `--surface-2` (white), `--surface-1` (card), `--surface-0` (page bg); role tints `--bg-{accent,danger,success,warning}` **Text**: `--text-primary` (black), `--text-secondary` (muted), `--text-muted` (hints); role `--text-{accent,danger,success,warning}` **Borders**: `--border` (default hairline), `--border-strong` (hover), `--border-stronger`; role `--border-{accent,danger,success,warning}` **Typography**: `--font-sans`, `--font-voice` (serif), `--font-mono` **Layout**: `--radius` (8px), `--pad-{sm,md,lg,xl}`, `--gap-{xs,sm,md,lg,xl}`; for larger corners use literal `12px`/`16px` All auto-adapt to light/dark mode. For custom colors in HTML, use CSS variables. **Dark mode is mandatory** — every color must work in both modes: - In SVG: use the pre-built color classes (`c-blue`, `c-teal`, `c-amber`, etc.) for colored nodes — they handle light/dark mode automatically. Never write `<style>` blocks for colors. - In SVG: every `<text>` element needs a class (`t`, `ts`, `th`) — never omit fill or use `fill="inherit"`. Inside a `c-{color}` parent, text classes auto-adjust to the ramp. - In HTML: always use CSS variables (--text-primary, --text-secondary) for text. Never hardcode colors like color: #333 — invisible in dark mode. - Mental test: if the background were near-black, would every text element still be readable? ### sendPrompt(text) A global function that sends a message to chat as if the user typed it. Use it when the user's next step benefits from Claude thinking. Handle filtering, sorting, toggling, and calculations in JS instead. ### Links `<a href="https://...">` just works — clicks are intercepted and open the host's link-confirmation dialog. Or call `openLink(url)` directly. ## When nothing fits Pick the closest use case below and adapt. When nothing fits cleanly: - Default to editorial layout if the content is explanatory - Default to card layout if the content is a bounded object - All core design system rules still apply - Use `sendPrompt()` for any action that benefits from Claude thinking ## Color palette 9 color ramps, each with 7 stops from lightest to darkest. 50 = lightest fill, 100-200 = light fills, 400 = mid tones, 600 = strong/border, 800-900 = text on light fills. | Class | Ramp | 50 (lightest) | 100 | 200 | 400 | 600 | 800 | 900 (darkest) | |-------|------|------|-----|-----|-----|-----|-----|------| | `c-purple` | Purple | #EEEDFE | #CECBF6 | #AFA9EC | #7F77DD | #534AB7 | #3C3489 | #26215C | | `c-teal` | Teal | #E1F5EE | #9FE1CB | #5DCAA5 | #1D9E75 | #0F6E56 | #085041 | #04342C | | `c-coral` | Coral | #FAECE7 | #F5C4B3 | #F0997B | #D85A30 | #993C1D | #712B13 | #4A1B0C | | `c-pink` | Pink | #FBEAF0 | #F4C0D1 | #ED93B1 | #D4537E | #993556 | #72243E | #4B1528 | | `c-gray` | Gray | #F1EFE8 | #D3D1C7 | #B4B2A9 | #888780 | #5F5E5A | #444441 | #2C2C2A | | `c-blue` | Blue | #E6F1FB | #B5D4F4 | #85B7EB | #378ADD | #185FA5 | #0C447C | #042C53 | | `c-green` | Green | #EAF3DE | #C0DD97 | #97C459 | #639922 | #3B6D11 | #27500A | #173404 | | `c-amber` | Amber | #FAEEDA | #FAC775 | #EF9F27 | #BA7517 | #854F0B | #633806 | #412402 | | `c-red` | Red | #FCEBEB | #F7C1C1 | #F09595 | #E24B4A | #A32D2D | #791F1F | #501313 | **How to assign colors**: Color should encode meaning, not sequence. Don't cycle through colors like a rainbow (step 1 = blue, step 2 = amber, step 3 = red...). Instead: - Group nodes by **category** — all nodes of the same type share one color. E.g. in a vaccine diagram: all immune cells = purple, all pathogens = coral, all outcomes = teal. - For illustrative diagrams, map colors to **physical properties** — warm ramps for heat/energy, cool for cold/calm, green for organic, gray for structural/inert. - Use **gray for neutral/structural** nodes (start, end, generic steps). - Use **2-3 colors per diagram**, not 6+. More colors = more visual noise. A diagram with gray + purple + teal is cleaner than one using every ramp. - **Prefer purple, teal, coral, pink** for general diagram categories. Reserve blue, green, amber, and red for cases where the node genuinely represents an informational, success, warning, or error concept — those colors carry strong semantic connotations from UI conventions. (Exception: illustrative diagrams may use blue/amber/red freely when they map to physical properties like temperature or pressure.) **Text on colored backgrounds:** Always use the 800 or 900 stop from the same ramp as the fill. Never use black, gray, or --text-primary on colored fills. **When a box has both a title and a subtitle, they must be two different stops** — title darker (800 in light mode, 100 in dark), subtitle lighter (600 in light, 200 in dark). Same stop for both reads flat; the weight difference alone isn't enough. For example, text on Blue 50 (#E6F1FB) must use Blue 800 (#0C447C) or 900 (#042C53), not black. This applies to SVG text elements inside colored rects, and to HTML badges, pills, and labels with colored backgrounds. **Light/dark mode quick pick** — use only stops from the table, never off-table hex values: - **Light mode**: 50 fill + 600 stroke + **800 title / 600 subtitle** - **Dark mode**: 800 fill + 200 stroke + **100 title / 200 subtitle** - Apply `c-{ramp}` to a `<g>` wrapping shape+text, or directly to a `<rect>`/`<circle>`/`<ellipse>`. Never to `<path>` — paths don't get ramp fill. For colored connector strokes use inline `stroke="#..."` (any mid-ramp hex works in both modes). Dark mode is automatic for ramp classes. Available: c-gray, c-blue, c-red, c-amber, c-green, c-teal, c-purple, c-coral, c-pink. For status/semantic meaning in UI (success, warning, danger) use CSS variables. For categorical coloring in both diagrams and UI, use these ramps. ## SVG setup **ViewBox safety checklist** — before finalizing any SVG, verify: 1. Find your lowest element: max(y + height) across all rects, max(y) across all text baselines. 2. Set viewBox height = that value + 40px buffer. 3. Find your rightmost element: max(x + width) across all rects. All content must stay within x=0 to x=680. 4. For text with text-anchor="end", the text extends LEFT from x. If x=118 and text is 200px wide, it starts at x=-82 — outside the viewBox. Increase x or use text-anchor="start". 5. Never use negative x or y coordinates. The viewBox starts at 0,0. 6. **No unintentional overlaps.** For every pair of elements that aren't meant to layer (label-on-label, label-on-arrow, box-on-box, callout-on-shape), check their bounding boxes do not intersect. The only allowed overlaps are deliberate: a label centered inside its own box, an arrowhead touching the box it points to, a highlight rect behind the thing it highlights. If two unrelated elements would collide, move one — shorten the label, shift the y, add a row. A diagram with crossed labels reads as broken regardless of how good the content is. 7. summaries.summary: ロードマップ作成に向けて実装詳細と課題を整理した。

content.text:
TouchDesigner実装の知見を踏まえて、Unity移行後のロードマップを9フェーズで整理しました。7月〜12月で逆算すると、10〜11月の評価実験に間に合わせるには視点追従の実装を7月中に固めるのが分岐点になります。

**フェーズ1〜2（最優先・7月）**

視点追従がボトルネックです。TouchDesignerで発見済みの以下の癖はUnity側でも必ず再現するはずなので、実装前提として持ち込んでください。

- `left_ear`/`right_ear`ラベルの左右反転
- x/y座標の符号反転
- Z方向のEMAスムージング必須（高周波ノイズ）
- フレーム間差分への`max_delta`クランプ（暴走防止）

MediaPipe Unity Pluginの座標系がTouchDesignerのMediaPipe TOPと同じ規約かは未確認要素なので、まず生の`nose:x/y/z`、`left_ear`、`right_ear`をConsoleに出力し、TouchDesigner側で記録済みの数値範囲・符号と突き合わせるところから始めると手戻りが少ないです。`Camera.projectionMatrix`の非対称視錐台構成は、`Pansensitivity`/`Dollysensitivity`相当のパラメータを最初からインスペクタで調整可能にしておくと、後のチューニングが楽になります。

**フェーズ3〜4（8月）**

カエルモデルは変形パーツ分割（Body/Head/Eye×2/LegBack×2/LegFront×2）を先に決めてしまい、パーツごとにColliderを持たせておくと、フェーズ5のLeap Motion接触判定にそのまま接続できます。空間音響はSteam Audio Unity Pluginの`Steam Audio Source`/`Listener`を使えば、TouchDesignerの`Audio Render CHOP`（Simple Positional）相当の機能がコンポーネント単位で完結するので、実装コストはTouchDesigner版より下がるはずです。リスナー位置の更新スクリプトは`listenerHead`の耳中点計算ロジック（atan2による向き算出含む）をほぼそのまま移植できます。

**フェーズ5〜6（8月末〜9月）**

Leap Motion（Ultraleap Gemini/v5）の接触検出は、`Panthreshold`/`Dollythreshold`相当の閾値を外部パラメータ化しておくのが今回の設計方針と一致します。マルチモーダルフィードバック（`PlayOneShot`＋`LeanTween`/`DOTween`によるScale変形）はこのフェーズで両方同時に組んでしまうのが効率的です。

**フェーズ7〜9（9月末〜12月）**

統合テストで6要素（視点追従・音響・鳴き声・接触・変形・カメラ映像）を同時に動かした際のフレームレート低下が一番の懸念点です。特にMediaPipe処理とLeap Motion処理を同一フレームで回すと負荷が重なるので、早めに一度フル構成でのパフォーマンス計測をしておくと安心です。評価実験（SUS・NASA-TLX・Presence Questionnaire）は10〜11月に設定しているので、9月末には最低限デモ可能な状態にしておくのが目安になります。

まず着手すべきは、MediaPipe Unity Pluginを導入して`nose:x/y/z`と耳座標が期待通りに取れるかの確認です。ここでつまずくと後続フェーズ全体がずれるので、具体的な出力値や設定で詰まったら遠慮なく聞いてください。

name: 裸眼立体映像と空間音響のインタラクションシステム
summary:
**Conversation overview**

この会話は、大川研究室に所属するB4の学生（廣瀬琥伯氏、学籍番号23C1117）が、「空間音響を伴う裸眼立体映像インタラクションシステム」に関する卒業研究のサーベイ課題に向けて、関連する英語原著論文を探すことを目的として行われた。研究の構成要素は①ペッパーズゴースト方式による裸眼立体映像（天井型LCD＋45度ハーフミラー）、②MediaPipeを用いた視点追跡（頭部トラッキング）、③HRTFによる空間音響、④Leap Motionによるハンドインタラクション、⑤インテグラルイメージングによる複数人立体視、⑥接触時の物体変形フィードバックであり、TouchDesignerとGPU付きデスクトップPCで実装が進められている。スケジュールは5〜6月：環境構築、7〜9月：実装、10〜11月：実験・評価（SUS、NASA-TLX、Presence Questionnaire）、12月：論文執筆。

会話を通じて学生は複数の観点から論文を探すよう依頼した。最初に空間音響と奥行き知覚、Leap Motionによるハンドインタラクション全般を対象としたが、途中で「原著論文に限定してほしい」という明確な修正指示があった。その後、添付した笠井ら（IPSJ Interaction 2024）および笠井ら（UIST Adjunct 2025）の論文を起点として類似・関連研究を探すよう依頼し、さらにミラー反射型立体ディスプレイ（Fish Tank VR型）の研究系譜の調査へと発展した。最終的に研究の新規性として「視点追従（Fish Tank VR）×空間音響の統合的検証」を主軸とし、「低コストWebカメラ式装置への統合システムとしての新規性」を装置面の売りとして添えるという方向性が議論された上で、課題（未知語抽出＋要約）に使う最も有効な一本としてZahorik (2022) "Asymmetric visual capture of virtual sound sources in the distance dimension"（Frontiers in Neuroscience, DOI: 10.3389/fnins.2022.958577）が推薦された。

会話後半では、音響フィードバックは一旦置き「接触時に物体が変形する視覚フィードバック」に絞った論文調査に切り替えるよう指示があり、"Evaluation of Pseudo-Haptic Interactions with Soft Objects in Virtual Environments"（PLOS ONE, 2016, PMC4924842）が最重要論文として特定された。研究全体を通じてキーとなる専門用語として、visual capture、ventriloquist effect、pseudo-haptics、HRTF、motion parallax、integral imaging、fish tank VR、presence、UEQなどが繰り返し登場した。学生は音声入力を使用しており、「リープモーション」「糖分度（→奥行き度）」「直角的（→直感的）」「視覚（→聴覚の言い間違い）」など音声認識による誤変換が散見されたが、文脈から意図を補って対応した。

I need to summarize research content in Japanese, so I'm translating and condensing the key findings into a concise Japanese summary.# 研究概要：空間音響を伴う裸眼立体映像インタラクションシステム

**研究室・学生**：大川研究室 B4 23C1117 廣瀬琥伯

## 背景・目的
HMD型のAR機器はVR酔いや周囲との隔絶感、長時間装着時の身体的負担といった不快感が課題となっている。そこで本研究では、**裸眼立体表現**と**直感的なインタラクション**の実現を目指す。

## 提案手法

**1. 裸眼立体映像装置の基本原理**
- 視点追跡（ヘッドトラッキング）：カメラで両目位置をリアルタイム検出し、観察者の視点に同期した動的3D映像を生成
- 天井型ディスプレイ配置：液晶ディスプレイを天面に置き3D空間をレンダリング
- ペッパーズ・ゴースト方式：斜め45度のハーフミラーで空中に虚像を投影

**2. 運動視差に同期する空間音響**
関連研究（Jiménez-Navarro et al., 2024）を参考に、視覚と聴覚の距離感情報を意図的にずらすことで奥行き知覚を音でコントロールする手法を導入。頭部位置に応じてHRTFを制御し、仮想物体の位置から音が聞こえるようにするとともに、物体に触れた際にその座標から音が鳴る「触覚的聴覚フィードバック」を実装する。

**3. 複数人立体視の実現**
レンズアレイを用いたインテグラルイメージング方式により、複数人が同時に異なる角度から立体像を視認・操作できるAR装置を目指す。3Dモデルを各レンズに対応する微小視点からサンプリングして要素画像列（EIs）を合成し、結像面とレンズアレイの距離を最適化することで奥行き感を強調する。

- **ハードウェア**：GPU付デスクトップPCへ移行し、MediaPipeによる視点・骨格検出の安定化、複雑なシェーダー対応、低遅延化を実現
- **光学系**：アクリル板に反射防止フィルムを貼付し、裏面反射による二重像を解消して視認性を向上
- **ソフトウェア**：Unity（処理が重く制約が大きい）からTouchDesignerへ開発環境を移行。Python/GLSLとの親和性が高く、センサーデータを低遅延で映像に反映可能に

- SUS（System Usability Scale）：使いやすさの評価
- NASA-TLX：操作時の認知的負荷
- Presence Questionnaire：「そこに物がある感」の5段階評価

裸眼でのAR/MR体験を実現し、製品展示、CAD-CAM、考古学・文化遺産保存、医療教育、エンターテインメントなど教育・研究分野への応用が期待される。

**① 視点追従・裸眼立体（Fish Tank VR）系 ― 研究の基礎理論として最重要**

  提案手法の「視点追跡」の理論的原点。装置の原理説明に直結する語彙（perspective projection, head-coupled, disparity など）が学べる。

**④ 空間音響による奥行き知覚（関連研究[3]の周辺論文）**
- *"AudioMiXR: Spatial Audio Object Manipulation with 6DoF for Sound Design in Augmented Reality"* (2024/2025) – 6DoF空間でのHRTF操作、視聴覚のずれによる知覚エラーの議論あり
- *"Auptimize: Optimal Placement of Spatial Audio Cues for Extended Reality"* (2024) – ventriloquist effect（腹話術効果）など、視覚と聴覚の位置ずれに関する重要な現象を扱う
- *"Impact of HRTF individualisation and head movements in a real/virtual localisation task"* (2025) – HRTFの個人化と頭部運動が音源定位に与える影響。触覚的聴覚フィードバックの設計根拠になりうる

## 選び方のアドバイス
1. **課題の目的（未知語抽出＋要約）に照らすと、Abstract/Introductionが専門用語密度高く、かつ本文が読みやすい査読付き会議論文（CHI, SIGGRAPH, ISMAR, IEEE TVCG）が最適**です。特許文書は言い回しが独特で単語抽出の教材としては不向きなので避けるのがおすすめです。
2. 自分の研究の「新規性」を語る上では、①のFish Tank VR系（視点追従の理論的系譜）と④の空間音響系（関連研究[3]の前後論文）を1本ずつ選ぶと、既存研究との差分が説明しやすくなります。
3. arXiv版がある論文（Auptimize、AudioMiXRなど）は無料で全文入手できるため、まずはそこから読み始めるのが効率的です。

どれか1本について詳しく内容を掘り下げたり、実際にPDFを取得して単語抽出のお手伝いをすることもできます。必要であれば言ってください。

## Description

### BACKGROUND

1. Field of the Description The present invention relates, in general, to projecting or displaying video/animated or still three dimensional (3D) images, and, more particularly, to autostereoscopy and autostereoscopic projection systems such as those adapted to display ghost or latent 3D images without requiring accurate tracking of a viewer's right and left eye or glasses, headgear, or other equipment that has to be worn or used by a viewer. 2. Relevant Background There are numerous entertainment and other settings where it is desirable to create a unique visual display. For example, theme or amusement parks may include rides or walk-through attractions where guests (or “viewers”) are entertained by a unique visual effect or illusion. Pepper's ghost is an illusionary technique used by magicians, by ride or attraction designers, and others to produce a 3D illusion of a latent or ghost-like image.

A sheet or piece of glass (e.g., a beam splitter) 118 is positioned at an angle (e.g., 45 degrees) between the scene 110 and the expected or planned position of the viewer 105 (or the viewer's point of view (POV)) or an outer display surface/window.

content.title: 3D Displays: Their Evolution, Inherent Challenges & Future Perspectives
content.text: Except for the immersive 3D GRDs, some prior researches also brought motion parallax to small-scale GRDs through tracking the viewer's position. During the first boom of HMDs, Deering adapted a CRT monitor into a 3D display [11]. The system was originally designed to solve the low Pixel Per Degree (PPD) problem of the HMDs at that time. The system was equipped with time-multiplexed eyewear and a head tracker that allowed seamless motion parallax and binocular parallax. A similar system was proposed next year by Ware et al [12]. Through the FTVR displays, viewers can move their heads within a restricted range while seeing a pair of off-axis stereo views. Therefore, Ware named this type of system as "Fish Tank VR" (FTVR) 3D displays. In 2018, an advanced adaption of the FTVR "Co-Globe" [13] was demonstrated on SIG-GRAPH. The display had a spherical projection plane as a screen and had 360 degrees viewing angle with motion parallax and binocular parallax.

We put forward the use of transparent 3D displays for augmented reality. For a glasses-free experience with autostereoscopy and a large viewing area, we study the use of a recent transparent display with multiple discrete and horizontally adjacent viewing zones. Although promising, this display cannot directly be used for augmented reality due to inconsistencies within and between the discrete viewing zones. In this work, we propose to overcome this limitation by tracking the user’s eyes for ensuring continuous transitions, thus making the display feasible for augmented reality. In particular, we compensate the intensity variations, we ensure a consistent horizontal parallax within and between the adjacent viewing zones, and we add vertical parallax.

content.text:
For a faithful virtual reproduction of spatialised sound sources, indiv

The objective of Audio Augmented Reality (AAR) applications are to seamlessly integrate virtual sound sources within a real environment. It is critical for these applications that virtual sources are localised precisely at the intended position, and that the acoustic environments are accurately matched. One effective method for spatialising sound on headphones is through Head-Related Transfer Functions (HRTFs). These characterise how the physical features of a listener modify sound waves before they reach the eardrum. This study examines the influence of using individualised HRTFs on the localisation and the perceived realism of virtual sound sources associated with a real visual object. Participants were tasked with localising virtual and real speech sources presented via headphones and through a spherical loudspeaker array, respectively. The assessment focussed on perceived realism and sources location.

検索してみたところ、この研究の4つの柱（①裸眼立体・視点追従、②ペッパーズゴースト方式、③複数人向けインテグラルイメージング、④空間音響による奥行き知覚）それぞれに対応する良質な論文が見つかりました。検索ワードと候補論文をまとめます。

## おすすめの検索ワード（英語）

| テーマ | 検索ワード例 |
|---|---|
| 視点追従・裸眼立体（基礎理論） | `"fish tank VR"`, `head-coupled perspective`, `motion parallax display`, `eye-coupled stereo display` |
| ペッパーズゴースト方式 | `Pepper's ghost autostereoscopic display`, `half-mirror floating image display` |
| 複数人向け立体視 | `multi-viewer autostereoscopic display`, `integral imaging multi-view AR`, `eye-tracked transparent autostereoscopic display` |
| 空間音響×奥行き知覚 | `HRTF depth perception AR`, `spatial audio virtual object interaction`, `sound-visual depth cue VR` |
| 評価手法 | `presence questionnaire virtual reality`, `NASA-TLX AR evaluation` |

Google Scholar・IEEE Xplore・ACM Digital Library では、上記ワードを2〜3語ずつ組み合わせて検索するのがおすすめです（例：`autostereoscopic display motion parallax interaction`）。

## 課題（未知語抽出・要約）に向いている候補論文

**① 視点追従・裸眼立体（Fish Tank VR）系 ― 研究の基礎理論として最重要**
- Ware, C. et al. (1993) *"Fish tank virtual reality"* – INTERACT/CHI'93
  提案手法の「視点追跡」の理論的原点。装置の原理説明に直結する語彙（perspective projection, head-coupled, disparity など）が学べる。
- Arsenault & Ware (2004) *"The Importance of Stereo and Eye-Coupled Perspective for Eye-Hand Coordination in Fish Tank VR"* – Presence: Teleoperators and Virtual Environments
  「直感的インタラクション」評価の先行研究として使いやすい。

**② ペッパーズゴースト × 裸眼立体**
- 学術論文としては特許（US8692738B2など）が多くヒットしますが、これは工学的原理の説明としては参考になっても学術サーベイの引用対象としてはやや弱いです。むしろ①③の論文の関連研究節（Related Work）内で "half-mirror" や "beam splitter" 3D display として触れられているものを辿るのが効率的です。

**③ 複数人立体視・インテグラルイメージング系**
- Schlick, Crespel, Granier, Reuter (2022) *"A Hybrid Multi-view and Eye-tracked Transparent Autostereoscopic Display for Augmented Reality"* – London Imaging Meeting
  「複数人立体視の実現」の章と最も近い内容。トラッキングと多視点表示の両立という課題設定が一致。
- *"Multi-viewer tracking integral imaging system and its viewing zone analysis"* – Optics Express
  インテグラルイメージングの要素画像（EIs）生成の技術的核心を扱っており、Fig.2の説明部分と対応。

**④ 空間音響による奥行き知覚（関連研究[3]の周辺論文）**
- *"AudioMiXR: Spatial Audio Object Manipulation with 6DoF for Sound Design in Augmented Reality"* (2024/2025) – 6DoF空間でのHRTF操作、視聴覚のずれによる知覚エラーの議論あり
- *"Auptimize: Optimal Placement of Spatial Audio Cues for Extended Reality"* (2024) – ventriloquist effect（腹話術効果）など、視覚と聴覚の位置ずれに関する重要な現象を扱う
- *"Impact of HRTF individualisation and head movements in a real/virtual localisation task"* (2025) – HRTFの個人化と頭部運動が音源定位に与える影響。触覚的聴覚フィードバックの設計根拠になりうる

## 選び方のアドバイス
1. **課題の目的（未知語抽出＋要約）に照らすと、Abstract/Introductionが専門用語密度高く、かつ本文が読みやすい査読付き会議論文（CHI, SIGGRAPH, ISMAR, IEEE TVCG）が最適**です。特許文書は言い回しが独特で単語抽出の教材としては不向きなので避けるのがおすすめです。
2. 自分の研究の「新規性」を語る上では、①のFish Tank VR系（視点追従の理論的系譜）と④の空間音響系（関連研究[3]の前後論文）を1本ずつ選ぶと、既存研究との差分が説明しやすくなります。
3. arXiv版がある論文（Auptimize、AudioMiXRなど）は無料で全文入手できるため、まずはそこから読み始めるのが効率的です。

content.title: Thinking Outside the Lab: VR Size & Depth Perception in the Wild
content.text:
# 2.2 Perception Studies in Immersive VR

Presenting a virtual space that can be accurately perceived by human eyes is important for VR applications to be more immersive and useful. In contrast to the somewhat contradictory results about depth and size perception in the real world, research on egocentric depth perception in VR has, in general, found a tendency of depth underestimation [61] and size underconstancy [29, 37]. In a study replicating the real-world experiment of Lappin et al. [42] in a virtual setting [3], participants placed the perceived mid-points closer than the true mid-points, in contrast to the antiforeshortening effect observed by Lappin et al. in the real-world setting. Corujeira and Oakley [7] also found depth underestimation in VR using a blind walking protocol. They further pointed out the effect of eye height on depth perception accuracy; a lying-on-the-floor eye height of 20 cm led to more accurate judgements than when seated (110 cm). 

Size-matching studies in VR have found underestimation of distant object sizes [29, 37, 38], largely compatible with results from studies on depth perception.

In addition to the differences in the general tendency of biases from the real world, depth perception in VR has also been found to be less precise (higher depth discrimination threshold) than in the real world [52]. This discrepancy between real and virtual environments has been of much research interest. We refer the reader to the survey by Renner et al. [61] for an in-depth review on the topic. The significant variability of available pictorial depth cues—such as texture [71], lighting [70], number of objects [38]—in different virtual environments could cause varying levels of distortion in perceived depth. The technical properties of current VR systems, such as FoV [35], IPD [4, 78], and vergence-accommodation conflict [27] may also affect depth perception accuracy.

### おすすめ検索ワード
`sound distance modulation depth perception`, `auditory feedback object presence VR`, `loudness cue distance perception virtual`, `ventriloquist effect AR audio-visual`, `binaural rendering distance realism`, `collision sound feedback virtual object`

### 候補論文
- **Villegas, J.** *"Locating Virtual Sound Sources at Arbitrary Distances in Real-Time Binaural Reproduction"* — Virtual Reality誌の特集号内。距離に応じた音の実時間レンダリング（音源が実際にそこにあるように聞こえる仕組み）の基礎論文。研究の「触れた座標から音が鳴る」設計の参考文献として直結する。
- **"Comparing auditory distance perception in real and virtual environments and the role of the loudness cue"**（ScienceDirect, 2024）
  音量の手がかりが音の距離知覚にどう寄与するかをERP（事象関連電位）で調べた研究で、実環境とVR環境を比較している。「実物感」を定量評価する手法として参考になる。
- **"Auptimize: Optimal Placement of Spatial Audio Cues for Extended Reality"**（2024, arXiv）
  視覚と音源位置のずれが30度以内であれば腹話術効果（音の発生源を実際とは違う場所にあると誤って知覚する現象）が働くことを報告しており、視覚と聴覚を意図的にずらす関連研究[3]の理解を補強する。
- **"Audio in VR: Effects of a Soundscape and Movement-Triggered Step Sounds on Presence"**（Frontiers, 2020）
  音の要素（環境音や移動に連動した足音）がPresence（そこにいる感覚）やRealismに大きな効果を持つことを実験的に示した研究。あなたの研究の評価指標（Presence Questionnaire）と直結する。
- **"Impact of HRTF individualisation and head movements in a real/virtual localisation task"**（2025, arXiv）
  個人化されたHRTFの使用が仮想音源の定位精度や知覚されるリアリズムにどう影響するかを検証した研究。頭部運動と音源定位の関係は、あなたの装置のヘッドトラッキングと音響制御の統合設計に応用可能。

## テーマ②：Leap Motion（ハンドトラッキング）による操作・インタラクション研究

### おすすめ検索ワード
`Leap Motion hand gesture interaction virtual reality`, `fingertip gesture recognition virtual environment`, `Leap Motion grasp manipulation`, `hand tracking mid-air interaction 3D`, `Leap Motion haptic feedback`

- **"Virtual Assembling Using Hand Tracking with Leap Motion Controller"**（IEEE, 2021）

- **"Fingertip Gestures Recognition Using Leap Motion and Camera for Interaction with Virtual Environment"**（MDPI, 2020）

A real-time system for sound spatialization via headphones is presented. 

Conventional headphone spatialization techniques effectively place sources on the surface of a virtual sphere around the listener. In the new system, sources can be spatialized at different distances from a listener by interpolating head-related impulse responses (HRIRs) measured between 20 and 160 cm. Subjective tests showed that such simplifications yield satisfactory spatialization for some angles and distances.

# Asymmetric visual capture of virtual sound sources in the distance dimension

**DOI:** 10.3389/fnins.2022.958577

**Published:** 2022-09-01

**Authors:** Pavel Zahorik

**Affiliations:** ^1^Department of Otolaryngology and Communicative Disorders, Heuser Hearing Institute, University of Louisville, Louisville, KY, United States; ^2^Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, University of Louisville, Louisville, KY, United States

**Keywords:** visual capture, ventriloquist effect, sound localization, spatial hearing, multisensory, distance, perception, computational model

## Abstract

Visual capture describes the tendency of a sound to be mislocalized to the location of a plausible visual target. This effect, also known as the ventriloquist effect, has been extensively studied in humans, but primarily for mismatches in the angular direction between auditory and visual targets. 

Here, visual capture was examined in the distance dimension using a single visual target (an un-energized loudspeaker) and invisible virtual sound sources presented over headphones. The sound sources were synthesized from binaural impulse-response measurements at distances ranging from 1 to 5 m (0.25 m steps) in the semi-reverberant room (7.7 × 4.2 × 2.7 m^3^) in which the experiment was conducted. Listeners (*n* = 11) were asked whether or not the auditory target appeared to be at the same distance as the visual target. Within a block of trials, the visual target was placed at a fixed distance of 1.5, 3, or 4.5 m, and the auditory target varied randomly from trial-to-trial over the sample of measurement distances. The resulting psychometric functions were generally consistent with visual capture in distance, but the capture was asymmetric: Sound sources behind the visual target were more strongly captured than sources in front of the visual target.

content.text:
# Speaker Placement Agnosticism: Improving the Distance-based Amplitude Panning Algorithm

Jacob Sundstrom

Department of Music

University of California, San Diego

La Jolla, California, USA

jsundst@ucsd.edu

Abstract-Lossius et. al introduced the distance-based amplitude panning algorithm, or DBAP, to enable flexibility of loudspeaker placement in artistic and scientific contexts. The algorithm allows for arbitrary loudspeaker locations in a 2D plane so that a virtual sound source may navigate the 2D space. The gains for each speaker are calculated as a function of the source's distance to each loudspeaker, thus creating a sound field. This gives the listener the impression of a source moving through the field of loudspeakers. This paper introduces a heuristically developed robust variation of DBAP that corrects for faulty assumptions in the implementation of Lossius.

content.text:
The realism and immersion of Virtual Reality (VR) experiences depend on the quality of interactions between the virtual hand and virtual objects. The current drawbacks, such as seemingly artificial hand-object interactions and erratic post-collision behaviors of both virtual objects and the virtual hand, curtail the effectiveness of VR in tasks requiring precise manipulation, precluding sustained and successful adoption of VR in precision manual tasks. To address these limitations, we advocate a strategic approach across three related domains: (1) Developing a sufficiently realistic virtual hand model (i.e., a set of rigid bodies or deformable meshes) that can implement the complex movements of a biological hand. (2) Exploiting synergistic patterns of multi-digit motion and contact forces revealed by research on neuroscience, psychophysics, and manual actions to develop hand-object collision handling algorithms.

#### 2 Related Works

## 2.1 Haptic Feedback for Virtual Object Interactions

Kinesthetic haptic feedback has been broadly studied to enrich virtual object interactions and has shown improved realism, immersion, presence, and performance [14, 45]. Realistic haptic feedback that matches the user's expectation based on real-life experience also increases body ownership [10]. Consequently, kinesthetic feedback has shown its effectiveness in virtual applications requiring information on the virtual object's physical properties, such as bone surgery training [12] and virtual collaboration involving moving a virtual object together [2].

Unlike vibrotactile feedback, which only affects the skin surface, kinesthetic feedback also engages muscles and joints. This deeper engagement has led to the development of different form factors, methods, and devices to provide such feedback realistically.

content.title: Exploring the Role of Expected Collision Feedback in Crowded Virtual   Environments
content.text:
This paper studies the impact of the expected collision feedback on user perception and interaction with virtual crowds. We examine the effectiveness of commonly used collision feedback techniques (auditory cues and tactile vibrations) as well as inducing participants to expect that a physical bump with a real person might occur, as if some virtual humans actually correspond to real persons embodied into them and sharing the same physical space. Our results indicate that the expected collision feedback significantly influences both participant behavior—encompassing global navigation and local movements—and subjective perceptions of presence and copresence. Specifically, the introduction of a perceived risk of actual collision was found to significantly impact global navigation strategies and increase the sense of presence. Auditory cues had a similar effect on global navigation and additionally enhanced the sense of copresence. 

By using a VR headset, the user can be embodied into a virtual avatar [29], gaining an illusion of body ownership over it, feeling present (sense of presence) in the virtual world and having the experience of being part of the virtual crowd.

Presence can be seen as the addition of place illusion (PI) and plausibility (Psi) [39, 40]. PI is the illusion of being in the place depicted by the VR. Psi is the illusion that the virtual situation and events are really happening. While PI can be achieved in VR through natural sensorimotor contingencies integrated by the hardware on sensory outputs [24], Psi is a far more complex and interesting aspect to study since any unexpected event can produce a break in presence or a failure of expectations in the participant. Similarly, copresence refers to the extent to which a participant has the illusion of being there with other participants [10].

content.title: Exploring cross-modal perception in a virtual classroom: the effect of visual stimuli on auditory selective attention
content.text:
In virtual reality research, distinguishing between auditory and visual influences on perception has become increasingly challenging. To study auditory selective attention in more close-to-real-life settings, an auditory task was adapted to a virtual classroom. The new environment suggested evidence of increased attention, possibly introduced by the visual representation, gamification effects, and immersion. This could engage participants more effectively. To delve deeper into the impact of cross-modal effects, the paradigm was extended by visual stimuli. Participants were initially tasked with directing their auditory attention to a cued spatial position and categorizing animal names played from that position while ignoring distracting sounds. Animal pictures introduced in Experiment 1 were either congruent or incongruent with the auditory target stimuli, thus either supporting or competing with the auditory information. 

Numerous studies have shown that even task-irrelevant visual stimuli can facilitate auditory perception, for example, by improving spatial localization, loudness perception, or frequency discrimination. A comprehensive overview of these effects is provided by [56]. However, such effects are rarely examined in scenarios that combine realistic environments with experimental control.

To understand real-world, cross-modal effects, many researchers create virtual reality (VR) scenarios, which balance real-world likeness and experimental control. Although there is a clear trend toward using the technology for psychological research ([45]), the impact of the virtual environment and the usually head-worn hardware on cognition is not yet fully understood. This uncertainty makes VR an interesting research platform for exploring ASA in settings that are both controlled and realistic.

content.title: Metal Sounds Stiffer than Drums for Ears, but Not Always for Hands: Low-Level Auditory Features Affect Multisensory Stiffness Perception More than High-Level Categorical Information
content.text:
To understand whether there is any interaction between auditory and haptic stiffness perception, and if so, whether the inferred material category is the most relevant auditory information, we conducted experiments using a force-feedback device and the modal synthesis method to present haptic stimuli and impact sound in accordance with participants’ actions, and to modulate low-level acoustic parameters, i.e., frequency and damping, without changing the inferred material categories of sound sources. We found that metal sounds consistently induced an impression of stiffer surfaces than did drum sounds in the audio-only condition, but participants haptically perceived surfaces with modulated metal sounds as significantly softer than the same surfaces with modulated drum sounds, which directly opposes the impression induced by these sounds alone. 

However, the audio inputs used in roughness experiments have been mostly band-limited noise or sounds of rubbing sandpaper, which do not include object information such as material composition, object shape, or size. Audio-haptic interaction with abundant information on sound sources inferred from acoustic signals was not explored in these studies.

In the field of virtual reality, researchers have noticed the influence of sound on the haptic stiffness sensation [[15]–[17]]. The rankings of the stiffness of simulated haptic surfaces when presented along with recorded or synthesized sounds increased with the auditory stiffness. Recent work has shown that when no tactile cues were available, the audio feedback of a tapping action made participants perceive that the tapped virtual surface was softer for weak sounds [[18]]. Auditory information might also affect the perception of body parts [[19]].

In this paper, we investigate the perceptual interaction between stereoscopy, surface deformation, and haptic feedback in the condition of active touch implemented using friction modulation based on ultrasonic vibrations. The experimental study is based on a Visual-Tactile exploration of a virtual texture. Our objective is to understand the interaction of one modality over the other for roughness and depth perception. Participants were asked to make visual and tactile texture roughness judgments and to estimate the depth of deformation of the texture below their fingers. 

Our results suggest that: 1) perceived tactile roughness can be modified by adding stereoscopic rendering and/or visual surface deformation but only for smooth tactile textures, 2) perceived visual roughness can be modified by increasing the tactile roughness, 3)the overall roughness (Visual + Tactile) is mainly impacted by the tactile perception.

content.title: Visuo-Tactile based Predictive Cross Modal Perception for Object   Exploration in Robotics
content.text:
# Visuo-Tactile based Predictive Cross Modal Perception for Object Exploration in Robotics

Anirvan Dutta, Etienne Burdet and Mohsen Kaboli

Abstract—Autonomously exploring the unknown physical properties of novel objects such as stiffness, mass, center of mass, friction coefficient, and shape is crucial for autonomous robotic systems operating continuously in unstructured environments. We introduce a novel visuo-tactile based predictive cross-modal perception framework where initial visual observations (shape) aid in obtaining an initial prior over the object properties (mass). The initial prior improves the efficiency of the object property estimation, which is autonomously inferred via interactive non-prehensile pushing and using a dual filtering approach. The inferred properties are then used to enhance the predictive capability of the cross-modal function efficiently by using a human-inspired 'surprise' formulation.

# B. Cognitive Limitations

Through examination of the physiological, psychophysical and neurological aspects of human interactions, researchers have developed guidelines to ensure that visuo-haptic interactions will maintain this sense of realism. In order for the haptic signals to be perceived as distinct, these guidelines require that they occur at least 5.5ms apart. Additionally, these guidelines suggest that it may not be possible to perceive an individual ordering of signals if they are less than 20ms apart [13].

The impact of network impairments can be altered by cross-modal influences. Recent experimental work studies the influence of delay on the perception of surface stiffness in visual-haptic virtual environments. It was shown that delays in the visual modality alone caused an increase in perceived surface stiffness and that delays in the haptic modality alone caused a decrease in perceived surface stiffness.

## おすすめ検索ワード
`pseudo-haptics virtual deformation sound feedback`, `impact sound stiffness perception cross-modal`, `visual deformation haptic stiffness virtual`, `Leap Motion bare-hand grasping feedback`, `auditory feedback virtual touch realism presence`

## 原著論文（確認済み）

**1. Srinivasan, M. A., Beauregard, G. L., & Brock, D. (1996)**
*"The impact of visual information on the haptic perception of stiffness in virtual environments"* — Proc. 5th Annual Symposium on Haptic Interfaces for Virtual Environments and Teleoperator Systems
被験者がフォースフィードバック装置でバネを押しながら画面上でバネの変形（視覚的変形量）を見るという実験を行い、視覚情報が触覚的な硬さ知覚を上書きすることを実証した古典的原著論文。あなたの「変形によって実物感を与える」という着想の理論的基盤になる。

**2. "Metal Sounds Stiffer than Drums for Ears, but Not Always for Hands: Low-Level Auditory Features Affect Multisensory Stiffness Perception"**（PMC, 原著実験論文, DOI確認済み: PMC5130246）
フォースフィードバック装置とモーダル音響合成を用い、接触時の音（周波数・減衰特性）を操作することで、触覚的な硬さの知覚が音によって変化することを実験的に示した論文。**「接触時に音を鳴らして実物感を高める」というあなたの仮説を直接支持するデータ**を持つ、非常に重要な一次資料。

**3. "Cross-modal interaction of stereoscopy, surface deformation and tactile feedback on the perception of texture roughness in an active touch condition"**（ACM IHM 2023, DOI: 10.1145/3583961.3583967）
立体視（stereoscopy）、視覚的表面変形、触覚フィードバックの3つを組み合わせた実験研究で、**立体感（stereoscopy）と変形が知覚に与える影響**を検証しており、あなたの研究テーマ（立体視＋変形＋実物感）と最も構成が近い論文。

**4. "Enhancing hand-object interactions in virtual reality for precision manual tasks"**（*Virtual Reality*誌, Springer, 2024, DOI: 10.1007/s10055-024-01055-3）
変形可能なメッシュによる仮想手モデルと、多指の接触力パターンを利用した衝突判定アルゴリズムを提案。ハンドトラッキング下での物体変形表現の技術的手法として参考になる。

**5. "Evaluation of Visual Feedback Techniques for Virtual Grasping with Bare Hands using Leap Motion and Oculus Rift"**
Leap MotionとOculus Riftを用いた素手による把持実験で、衝突後の仮想物体・仮想手の振る舞いに対する視覚フィードバック手法を評価。Leap Motionを使う自分の研究環境と直接一致する。

content.title: Grabity: A virtual reality haptic controller for creating gravity and stiffness during grasping motions through asymmetric vibrations
content.text: In this invention, we introduce Grabity, a mobile, ungrounded haptic device, which can display various types of kinesthetic feedback to enhance the grasping and manipulating of virtual objects. This feedback includes gravity, force for inertia, as well as rigid stiffness force feedback between opposing fingers. The design combines a “gripper” style haptic device, for providing opposing forces between the index finger and thumb, and a skin deformation mechanism, for rendering inertia and mass of a virtual object. Asymmetric skin deformation enabled by linear vibratory motors can generate perceived virtual forces tangential to finger pads. In this invention, we apply this principle to render the virtual gravity force of different virtual masses, and their associated inertia in a 1 degree of freedom per finger. To create the sensation of gravity and inertia, we adapt two voice coil actuators to a mobile gripper type haptic device.

この論文（笠井・入山・小室, IPSJ Interaction 2024）と**論調・アプローチが近い原著論文**が見つかりました。特に1つ目は同じ著者による関連研究です。

## 特に注目すべき論文

**1. Kasai, Y., Iriyama, T., & Komuro, T. (2025)**
*"Deformation-based Visual Feedback for Grasping Manipulation of 3DUI Components"* — Adjunct Proceedings of the 38th Annual ACM Symposium on UIST
著者名（笠井・入山・小室）が一致しており、**アップロードされた論文の発展版・後続研究**とみられます。同じ「物体変形による視覚フィードバック」というテーマを3DUIコンポーネントの操作に拡張した内容と考えられ、まず最初に確認すべき論文です。

## 論調・アプローチが極めて近い原著論文

**2. "Effect of Virtual Hand's Fingertip Deformation on the Stiffness Perceived Using Pseudo-Haptics"**（VRST 2023, ACM, DOI: 10.1145/3611659.3615689）
仮想の手指先端の変形量を変えることで、被験者が物体の硬さ（硬い/柔らかい）をどう知覚するかを実験的に検証。**「手指の変形によって触覚的なリアリティを演出する」**という発想がアップロード論文と共通しており、次のステップ（変形の有用性評価実験）に直結する内容。

**3. "Evaluation of Pseudo-Haptic Interactions with Soft Objects in Virtual Environments"**（PLOS ONE, 2016, PMC4924842）
柔らかい物体表面の視覚的変形と、指し手（インデンタ）の速度制御を組み合わせて、物体の硬さ情報を疑似的に提示する手法を提案・評価した論文。触診（結節検出）タスクでの性能評価も行っており、**「変形フィードバックの有用性を実験で示す」**というアップロード論文の今後の課題と方向性が一致する。

**4. Prachyabrued, M. & Borst, C. W. (2014)**
*"Visual Feedback for Virtual Grasping"* — IEEE 3DUI（アップロード論文の参考文献[4]と同一）
手指のめり込み表現の有無について、透明化キューなど複数の視覚フィードバック手法を比較評価。アップロード論文が解決しようとしている「めり込み問題」そのものを扱った基礎研究。

**5. "Enhancing hand-object interactions in virtual reality for precision manual tasks"**（*Virtual Reality*誌, Springer, 2024, DOI: 10.1007/s10055-024-01055-3）
変形可能なメッシュを用いた仮想手モデルによって、手と物体の衝突後の不自然な振る舞い（めり込みなど）を改善するアプローチを包括的に論じたレビュー寄りの論文。関連研究の位置づけを整理するのに有用。

**6. Vosinakis, S. & Koutsabasis, P. (2018)**
*"Evaluation of Visual Feedback Techniques for Virtual Grasping with Bare Hands Using Leap Motion and Oculus Rift"* — *Virtual Reality*誌（アップロード論文の参考文献[2]と同一）
Leap Motionでの素手把持における視覚フィードバック手法（色変化・発光など）の有用性を比較評価した原著論文。

## 補足
論文中の参考文献[2][3][4][5]はいずれも同系統の「把持時の視覚フィードバック手法の比較評価」研究であり、あなたが今後行う予定の「変形の有無による把持性能・ユーザー選好の比較実験」を設計する際の実験デザインの参考になります。特に**論文1（同著者の後続研究）と論文2（フィンガー変形×硬さ知覚）**は、内容的にも手法的にも最も近い位置にあります。

どれかのPDFを取得して詳しく読み込む、あるいは未知語抽出を進めることもできます。必要であれば教えてください。

Abstract. 

We present a physically-based approach to grasping and manipulation of virtual objects that produces visually realistic results, addresses the problem of visual inter-penetration of hand and object models, and performs force rendering for force-feedback gloves, in a single framework. Our approach couples a simulation-controlled articulated hand model to tracked hand configuration using a system of linear and torsional virtual spring-dampers. We discuss an implementation of our approach that uses a widely available simulation tool for collision detection and response. We pictorially illustrate the resulting behavior of the virtual hand model and of grasped objects, discuss user behavior and difficulties encountered, and show that the simulation rate is sufficient for control of current force-feedback glove designs. We also present a prototype system for natural whole-hand interactions in a desktop-sized workspace.

I'm finding several papers from the same research group that used identical equipment—the spring hand model, CyberGlove, mirror-based display, and PhysX physics engine. The most foundational is Borst and Indugula's 2006 paper on spring-based whole-hand virtual grasping, which is directly what this study builds upon.

Then there's Prachyabrued and Borst's work on grasp release methods and visual interpenetration tradeoffs using the same apparatus, plus what appears to be a journal version of the uploaded paper in TVCG. These form a coherent body of work from the same lab exploring different aspects of the same virtual grasping system.

summaries.summary: 同じ研究グループの関連論文を特定しました。

content.text:
この論文（Prachyabrued & Borst, 2014）と**同一の装置構成（ミラー式立体ディスプレイ＋CyberGlove＋電磁トラッカー＋スプリングハンドモデル）**を用いた研究が、同じ研究グループ（University of Louisiana at Lafayette, CACS VR Lab）から複数見つかりました。これは装置の系譜そのものです。

## 装置の系譜として重要な論文（同一研究グループ）

**1. Borst, C. W. & Indugula, A. P. (2006)**
*"A Spring Model for Whole-Hand Virtual Grasping"* — *Presence: Teleoperators and Virtual Environments*, 15(1), 47-61
アップロード論文が採用している「スプリングハンドモデル（仮想手をバネで実手に追従させ、めり込みを防ぐ）」という装置原理そのものを最初に提案した根幹論文。デスクトップサイズの作業空間での素手インタラクション用プロトタイプシステムも提示しており、装置構成の直接の起源。

**2. Prachyabrued, M. & Borst, C. W. (2012)**
*"Virtual Grasp Release Method and Evaluation"* — *International Journal of Human-Computer Studies*, 70(11), 828-848
（拡張版："Dropping the Ball: Releasing a Virtual Grasp"）
同じスプリングハンドモデル・CyberGlove・ミラー式立体ディスプレイを使い、把持の「解放（リリース）」動作に着目した研究。装置構成はアップロード論文とほぼ同一。

**3. Prachyabrued, M. & Borst, C. W. (2012)**
*"Visual Interpenetration Tradeoffs in Whole-Hand Virtual Grasping"* — IEEE 3DUI（アップロード論文の参考文献[9]）
アップロード論文の直接の先行研究で、同じ装置（Cyberglove＋ミラー式ディスプレイ＋NVIDIA PhysX）を用いてIH（内側の手）とOH（外側の手）の2つの基本手法を比較。

**4. "Design and Evaluation of Visual Interpenetration Cues"**（IEEE TVCG, CACS VR Lab）
アップロード論文（IEEE 3DUI 2014版）の拡張ジャーナル版とみられ、同一装置・同一手法をより詳細に報告している可能性が高い論文。

## 装置構成が部分的に近い関連論文

**5. "DesktopGlove: A multi-finger force feedback interface separating degrees of freedom between hands"**
CyberGloveベースのデスクトップ規模の力覚フィードバック装置を扱っており、同じ研究グループの機材系譜に位置する。

**6. "Optical-Mechanical Motion Capture System for Virtual Reality Applications"**
CyberGloveと組み合わせた光学・機械式モーションキャプチャシステムに関する研究で、電磁トラッカーに代わるトラッキング手法の比較対象になりうる。

## 補足：装置面での重要ポイント
アップロード論文の装置は「**ミラー反射型の立体ディスプレイ（鏡＋偏光フィルム＋3Dメガネ）**」を使う、いわゆる**Fish Tank VR型**の構成です。これは前回紹介したWare (1993) “Fish tank virtual reality” の系譜とも重なるため、①**Fish Tank VR（視点追従＋立体表示）**の系譜と、②**CyberGlove＋スプリングハンドモデル（把持シミュレーション）**の系譜という2つの技術的系譜が組み合わさった装置だと理解すると、サーベイの構造が整理しやすくなります。

## ①系譜：黎明期の基礎研究（1990年代〜2000年代前半）

**起点となる論文**
- **Ware, C., Arthur, K., & Booth, K. S. (1993)** *"Fish tank virtual reality"* — CHI'93/INTERACT'93
  「Fish Tank VR」という用語を作った原典。視点追従とステレオ立体視の両方を検証する3つの実験を行い、視点追従（ヘッドカップリング）はステレオ立体視より3次元性の強い印象を与える上でより重要である可能性を示唆したという結論が、その後の研究の出発点になった。

- **Arthur, K. W., Booth, K. S., & Ware, C. (1993)** *"Evaluating 3D task-performance for fish tank virtual worlds"* — ACM Transactions on Information Systems
  木構造のトレース課題において、頭部追従を用いたステレオ表示は、追従なしの静的な表示と比べて誤答率が一桁改善するという結果を示し、その効果はステレオ単体による効果より顕著だったという、Fish Tank VRの有効性を定量的に証明した基礎論文。

- **Deering, M. (1992)** *"High resolution virtual reality"* — SIGGRAPH
  CRTモニタを用いた頭部追従立体視システムの先駆け。当時のHMDの解像度不足問題を解決するために考案され、時分割方式の眼鏡と頭部トラッカーを組み合わせて、シームレスな運動視差と両眼視差を実現した。あなたの研究の「視点追跡による動的3D映像生成」と直接つながる技術的源流。

**発展・拡張期**
- **Ware, C. & Franck, G. (1996)** *"Evaluating stereo and motion cues for visualizing information nets in three dimensions"* — ACM Transactions on Graphics
- **Mulder, J. D. & Van Liere, R. (2000)** *"Enhancing fish tank VR"* — 画面端での負の視差を持つ物体の奥行き知覚の混乱を減らすため、カドル（額縁的な視覚的枠組み）表示や頭部回転の増幅表現などの技術を提案した
- **Arsenault & Ware (2000)** — 目と手の協調動作においては、頭部追従の視点よりもステレオ立体視のほうが重要であることを示した研究で、Wareら自身の初期結論を精緻化した
- Demiralp et al. — CAVEとFish Tank VRの科学的可視化タスクにおける有用性比較

## ②装置面での発展（多視点・裸眼化）

あなたの研究に近い方向性として、**Fish Tank VRの「頭部追従」原理を裸眼立体（オートステレオ）ディスプレイに組み込む**研究群があります。
- **"Interscopic User Interface Concepts for Fish Tank Virtual Reality Systems"** — 裸眼立体視ディスプレイ技術に基づく新しいユーザーインターフェース概念を導入し、モーショントラッキングとオートステレオディスプレイを組み合わせて3次元データの対話的な入力・操作を実現した研究。まさにあなたの「視点追跡＋裸眼立体＋インタラクション」という構成と一致する。

## ③最新の研究動向（2024〜2026年）

**低コスト・アクセシブル化の潮流**
- **"Real-Time 3D Light-field Viewing with Eye-tracking on Conventional Displays"**（2025, arXiv）
  標準的な2Dモニタと一般的なRGBウェブカメラ、赤青アナグリフメガネのみを使い、リアルタイムアイトラッキングでライトフィールド画像をユーザーの頭部位置に動的に適応させるシステムを提案し、CPUのみで30FPSの安定動作を実現した。あなたが使っているMediaPipeベースの視点追跡と発想が非常に近い、まさに「最新版Fish Tank VR」。

- ウェブカメラとMediaPipe Face Meshを用いた**オープンソースの頭部追従型視差ディスプレイ**の開発も2025年に活発化しており、MediaPipe Face Meshによる顔認識、座標変換、One-Euroフィルタによる平滑化、非対称視錐台計算を組み合わせ、Three.jsやCSSのperspective-originを通じて画面を物理的な窓のように振る舞わせる実装が公開されている。研究というより実装コミュニティの動きだが、技術トレンドとして重要。

**知覚的リアリズムの追求**
- **Kim, D. et al. (2024)** *"Holographic parallax improves 3D perceptual realism"* — ACM Transactions on Graphics
  ホログラフィックディスプレイに運動視差を統合し、より自然な奥行き知覚を実現する研究。従来のFish Tank VR（視差のみ）を、より高度な光学技術（ホログラフィ）と融合させる方向性。

**多人数・広視野角化**
- 2018年にSIGGRAPHで発表された「Co-Globe」は、球面の投影スクリーンを持ち、360度の視野角で運動視差と両眼視差を提供する、FTVRの発展形として紹介されている。

## 新規性があると考えられる研究方向

これまでのFish Tank VR研究を俯瞰すると、**「視覚（視差・立体視）」単体の最適化に研究が集中しており、あなたが取り組んでいる「聴覚（空間音響）」「触覚的な変形フィードバック」との統合的な検証はほぼ手つかず**です。具体的には：

1. **視点追従×空間音響の統合的な知覚評価**
Fish Tank VRの研究はすべて視覚的な運動視差・立体視の効果検証にとどまっており、頭部位置に連動した音源のHRTF制御を同時に組み込んで「視覚と聴覚の運動視差」を統合評価した研究は見当たりません。Ware(1993)の「視点追従はステレオより重要」という古典的知見が、聴覚的な奥行き手がかりを加えた場合にも成り立つのかは、まだ検証されていない問いです。

2. **複数人インテグラルイメージング×個別空間音響のマルチモーダル奥行き提示**
複数人が同時に異なる角度から立体像を見られる装置（インテグラルイメージング）に対して、各視聴者ごとに異なる方向から音が聞こえるような個別化された空間音響を重ねる研究は、管見の限り存在しません。「1人称のFish Tank VR」から「複数人称のFish Tank VR＋個別音響」への拡張は新規性が高いと考えられます。

3. **低コストWebカメラ式Fish Tank VR＋接触変形＋接触音のフルマルチモーダル統合**
最新の研究トレンド（MediaPipeベースの低コストFish Tank VR）と、あなたがすでに調査している「接触時の物体変形」「接触音による実物感向上」を、単一の安価な装置（Webカメラ＋ペッパーズゴースト）に統合した研究は見当たりません。既存研究は「視覚のみ」「触覚のみ」「音響のみ」を個別に評価する傾向が強く、これらを同一の裸眼立体装置上でシステム化し、SUS・NASA-TLX・Presence Questionnaireで統合評価するアプローチ自体が新規性を持ちうるでしょう。

To address this, we propose a low-cost system that enables real-time 3D light-field viewing using only a standard 2D monitor, a conventional RGB webcam, and red-cyan anaglyph glasses. The system integrates real-time eye-tracking to dynamically adapt the displayed light-field image to the user’s ...

Creating immersive 3D visual experiences typically requires expensive and specialized hardware such as VR headsets, autostereoscopic displays, or active shutter glasses. These constraints limit the accessibility and everyday use of 3D visualization technologies in resource-constrained settings. To address this, we propose a low-cost system that enables real-time 3D light-field viewing using only a standard 2D monitor, a conventional RGB webcam, and red-cyan anaglyph glasses. The system integrates real-time eye-tracking to dynamically adapt the displayed light-field image to the user’s head position with a lightweight rendering pipeline that selects and composites stereoscopic views from pre-captured light-field data. The resulting anaglyph image is updated in real-time, creating a more immersive and responsive 3D experience. The system operates entirely on CPU and maintains a stable frame rate of 30 FPS, confirming its feasibility on typical consumer-grade hardware.

Light-field imaging [20, 11] has emerged as a powerful method for capturing and representing 3D content by recording the direction and intensity of light rays from a scene. Unlike traditional 2D photographs, which capture a flat image from a single viewpoint, light-field images preserve the spatial structure of a scene, enabling advanced features such as refocusing, viewpoint interpolation, and depth estimation. This makes light-field content particularly suitable for stereoscopic or autostereoscopic displays, where dynamic view rendering is essential for delivering convincing depth perception. From a practical standpoint, light-field acquisition has become increasingly user-friendly due to advances in both hardware and software. Commercial light-field cameras like the Lytro Illum [23] and Raytrix R-series [31] have popularized microlens array technology, where a dense array of small lenses is placed in front of the image sensor to capture multiple perspectives of the scene.

The development of 3D visualization technologies has produced a rich spectrum of systems that differ in terms of immersion, accessibility, and visual fidelity. These systems can generally be categorized into immersive head-mounted, glasses-free (autostereoscopic), and glasses-based stereoscopic solutions [9, 10]. HMDs used in VR and AR provide fully immersive 3D experiences by enclosing the user’s field of view and tracking head movement. Devices like the Meta Quest 3 [25], HTC Vive [16], and Microsoft HoloLens [26] enable rich interactivity and spatial immersion by combining stereoscopic rendering with six degrees of freedom (6DoF) motion tracking. These systems provide excellent depth cues including motion parallax, and stereo disparity, but are often constrained by high cost, user discomfort, and content development overhead [24, 19]. Autostereoscopic displays or glasses-free displays offer 3D visualization without requiring users to wear glasses.

State-of-the-art eye-tracking, stereo 3D format compatibility, accessibility and the complete elimination of setup times make the system a true game changer when it comes to displaying existing 3D data. With ZVIEW, existing 3D models and projects are presented in the simplest way and experienced spatially without VR glasses. Geometrically complex situations are captured at first glance as if the model were physically present. During virtual inspections, a reliable assessment of the spatial depth of the planning model is possible through optically distortion-free reproduction. The ZVIEW-28″ is an eye-tracking based autostereoscopic 3D display and is therefore only suitable for one person. ... SingleView AS3D displays, like MultiView AS3D displays, have lenticular optics, but due to the integrated eye-tracking, which captures the eye position of the user, only 2 instead of 5-9 perspective views of a content are required. As a result, ZVIEW is compatible with existing stereo content and applications. This opens up a multitude of application areas in which everything already happens virtually and in 3D. The left and right partial image are permanently and latency-free aligned on the display via the position detection of the viewer’s eyes in such a way that each eye only sees the specific partial image. Autostereoscopic displays deliver 3D effects without requiring the viewer to wear any special devices such as shutter glasses. For them to work, the eyes must be in the optimal position, which limits the viewer’s freedom of movement. To make sure viewers can enjoy the 3D experience without such restrictions, face tracking can be used. The illusion of depth in an image is achieved by using special screen-based technologies, inspired by our own visual system. Human brain extracts the depth information by fusing together two separate images acquired by our eyes. Similarly, autostereoscopic displays present a different image to each eye. The most popular way to achieve that is the parallax barrier. It’s a series of transparent strips that allow each eye to see different regions of the display screen. The “right eye” image is sent to the right eye, and the “left eye” image is sent to the left eye, creating a 3D effect.

Furthermore, various occlusions can often occur during the use of the system. This includes glasses, jewelry, tattoos, hair, beards, or any other object that can obstruct the viewer’s face or a part of the face. Such occlusions can be temporary, occurring for a short period of time. For example, the viewer can briefly scratch their face with their hand. They can also be permanent – for example, significant facial hair or tattoos. The tracker should be trained to handle such occlusions as efficiently as possible. Finally, the hardware used for autostereoscopic displays cannot be too expensive. This means that the tracker should work well with mainstream hardware, such as webcams. A reliable tracker can help provide realistic 3D effects without sacrificing user experience. However, in choosing the right tracker for autostereoscopic displays, it’s important to check whether it meets the necessary requirements.

A great viewing experience means that viewers are able to move freely and enjoy the best image quality at all times. However, movement can be a challenge for autostereoscopic displays, since they need to project a different image to each eye. To overcome this challenge, manufacturers are relying on face tracking. By tracking head position, eye position and even gaze direction, the system can render the video in respect to the viewer’s current view point. For the viewers, it means that they can move freely in front of the 3D display and enjoy the content regardless of their position. The tracker has to meet specific requirements when it comes to auto 3D displays. Otherwise, the video will not be rendered properly. First of all, the tracker must be quick and efficient. It must be able to detect and start tracking human faces as soon as they appear in front of the display; for example, when a new viewer appears or when the existing one leaves and then comes back again.

In 2009, USC ICT researchers presented a telepresence system [5] that used structured light for 3D acquisition and a volumetric 3D display. The system provided real-time capture, nearly continuous points of view and required no tracking markers or glasses, but capture and display were limited to a head-size volume. In 2010, Holografika introduced a compelling system [6] consisting of a large array of projectors and cameras offering fully dynamic real-time 3D capture and tracker-less autostereo display. The system, however, featured only a moderate capture rate (10–15 Hz) and did not offer fully continuous points of view – interpolation was performed between a linear array of densely placed 2D cameras and only horizontal parallax was provided. Featuring 27 cameras, three PCs, and scores of projectors, it was also a very expensive system to build.

content.title: Autostereoscopic Display: The Future of Glasses-Free 3D is Here – INAIRSPACE
content.text:
Pushing the boundaries even further are volumetric displays. While often grouped under the autostereoscopic umbrella, they represent a different approach altogether. Instead of presenting a flat 2D image that simulates depth through binocular cues, a true volumetric display actually creates imagery in three physical dimensions. Some systems use a rotating screen to rapidly spin a LED-lit panel, using persistence of vision to "draw" a 3D shape in mid-air. Others might use laser beams to project points of light onto a fog or within a transparent solid. The result is a truly holographic-looking image that can be viewed from virtually any angle without any special glasses. While currently limited in resolution, color, and commercial availability, they represent the holy grail of 3D visualization—a digital object that exists in our space as surely as a coffee mug on a table.

Imagine a world where digital content leaps out of the screen with breathtaking depth and realism, yet you don’t need to fumble for special glasses or awkward headgear. This isn't a glimpse into a distant sci-fi future; it is the tangible, evolving present promised by autostereoscopic display technology. For decades, 3D visualization has captivated audiences, but the requirement for accessories has always been a significant barrier, a tether to a less immersive experience. Autostereoscopic displays sever that tether, offering a window into a volumetric world that feels both magical and intuitively natural. The journey from the flickering anaglyph images of the past to the sophisticated, eye-tracking marvels of today is a story of relentless innovation, one that is quietly revolutionizing fields from medical surgery to automotive design. This technology is poised to fundamentally alter our relationship with visual information, moving us from passive viewers to active participants in a t

At its core, the goal of any stereoscopic display is to deliver a unique image to each of the viewer's eyes, tricking the brain into perceiving depth. Traditional stereoscopic methods, like those used in cinemas, rely on external aids—polarized or active shutter glasses—to filter the correct image to the correct eye. Autostereoscopic displays achieve this same feat without any intermediaries, weaving their magic directly through the screen itself. The term itself is a giveaway: 'auto' meaning self, and 'stereoscopic' meaning solid form. It is a display that creates the illusion of three dimensions by itself. The most common and historically significant method for accomplishing this is through the use of a parallax barrier. Imagine a incredibly fine grating, similar to a venetian blind, placed in front of an LCD layer. This barrier is precisely engineered to block light from certain angles.

Simple two-view autostereoscopic systems have a critical limitation: the viewer must remain in a very specific position to experience the 3D effect. Move slightly left or right, and the illusion can break, resulting in a confusing or inverted image. To overcome this, engineers developed multi-view autostereoscopic displays. These systems do not just encode two images (left and right); they encode many more—often 8, 9, 16, or even more discrete views of the same scene. Under a lenticular lens, for instance, instead of having two columns of pixels per lenticle (one for each eye), there might be eight or nine. The lens then projects these eight or nine different views into eight or nine corresponding zones in the viewing space. As a viewer moves horizontally in front of the screen, their eyes smoothly transition from one viewing zone to the next, receiving a continuously changing perspective of the 3D object.

Pushing the boundaries even further are volumetric displays. While often grouped under the autostereoscopic umbrella, they represent a different approach altogether. Instead of presenting a flat 2D image that simulates depth through binocular cues, a true volumetric display actually creates imagery in three physical dimensions. Some systems use a rotating screen to rapidly spin a LED-lit panel, using persistence of vision to "draw" a 3D shape in mid-air. Others might use laser beams to project points of light onto a fog or within a transparent solid. The result is a truly holographic-looking image that can be viewed from virtually any angle without any special glasses. While currently limited in resolution, color, and commercial availability, they represent the holy grail of 3D visualization—a digital object that exists in our space as surely as a coffee mug on a table.

Autostereoscopy is the display of stereoscopic imagery, typically two-view stereoscopic imagery, in a way that doesn't require special glasses or headgear. Because headgear is not required, it is also called "glasses-free 3D" or "glassesless 3D". There are two broad approaches currently used to accommodate motion parallax and wider viewing angles: eye-tracking, and multiple views so that the display does not need to sense where the viewer's eyes are located. Examples of autostereoscopic displays technology include lenticular lens, parallax barrier, and integral imaging. Volumetric and holographic displays are also autostereoscopic, as they produce a different image to each eye, although some do make a distinction between those types of displays that create a vergence-accommodation conflict and those that do not. Autostereoscopic displays based on parallax barrier and lenticular methodologies have been known for about 100 years.

A parallax barrier is a device placed in front of an image source, such as a liquid crystal display, to allow it to show a stereoscopic image or multiscopic image without the need for the viewer to wear 3D glasses. The principle of the parallax barrier was independently invented by Auguste Berthier, who published first but produced no practical results, and by Frederic E. Ives, who made and exhibited the first known functional autostereoscopic image in 1901. About two years later, Ives began selling specimen images as novelties, the first known commercial use. In the early 2000s, Sharp developed the electronic flat-panel application of this old technology to commercialization, briefly selling two laptops with the world's only 3D LCD screens. These displays are no longer available from Sharp but are still being manufactured and further developed from other companies.

Many organizations have developed autostereoscopic 3D displays, ranging from experimental displays in university departments to commercial products, and using a range of different technologies. The method of creating autostereoscopic flat panel video displays using lenses was mainly developed in 1985 by Reinhard Boerner at the Heinrich Hertz Institute (HHI) in Berlin. Prototypes of single-viewer displays were already being presented in the 1990s, by Sega AM3 (Floating Image System) and the HHI. Nowadays, this technology has been developed further mainly by European and Japanese companies. One of the best-known 3D displays developed by HHI was the Free2C, a display with very high resolution and very good comfort achieved by an eye tracking system and a seamless mechanical adjustment of the lenses. Eye tracking has been used in a variety of systems in order to limit the number of displayed views to just two, or to enlarge the stereoscopic sweet spot.

content.text:
We propose an image-based 3D display with motion parallax using face tracking. Multi-view images of target objects are recorded in advance by utilizing a camera mounted on a 6 DOF manipulator.

We propose an image-based 3D display with motion parallax using face tracking. Multi-view images of target objects are recorded in advance by utilizing a camera mounted on a 6 DOF manipulator. The 3D viewpoint of the user is measured by using a real-time non-contact face measurement system. One of the multi-view images is projected according as the camera position corresponding to the viewpoint of the user. The user can obtain 3D information of the object through a standard monitor by moving his/her head. A prototype system is developed and the consistency of the proposed method is confirmed by comparing generated images with captured images at the same viewpoints.

content.title: 3D Displays: Their Evolution, Inherent Challenges & Future Perspectives
content.text: Except for the immersive 3D GRDs, some prior researches also brought motion parallax to small-scale GRDs through tracking the viewer's position. During the first boom of HMDs, Deering adapted a CRT monitor into a 3D display [11]. The system was originally designed to solve the low Pixel Per Degree (PPD) problem of the HMDs at that time. The system was equipped with time-multiplexed eyewear and a head tracker that allowed seamless motion parallax and binocular parallax. A similar system was proposed next year by Ware et al [12]. Through the FTVR displays, viewers can move their heads within a restricted range while seeing a pair of off-axis stereo views. Therefore, Ware named this type of system as "Fish Tank VR" (FTVR) 3D displays. In 2018, an advanced adaption of the FTVR "Co-Globe" [13] was demonstrated on SIG-GRAPH. The display had a spherical projection plane as a screen and had 360 degrees viewing angle with motion parallax and binocular parallax.
